report.answer_text:
What it is: Lenacapavir is an HIV-1 capsid inhibitor.[1] It is a long-acting antiviral made by Gilead Sciences. It was first approved to treat HIV-1 infection under the brand name Sunlenca in 2022.[1]
What the FDA approved in 2025: On June 18, 2025, the FDA approved Gilead's Yeztugo (lenacapavir) to reduce the risk of sexually acquired HIV infection. The approval covers adults and adolescents who weigh at least 35 kg and are at risk of acquiring HIV.[2] This use is called pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP. It was billed as the first and only FDA-approved HIV prevention option offering 6 months of protection.[3]
How it's given:
Starting doses are two subcutaneous injections plus two oral tablets on day 1, then two more tablets on day 2.[4]
After that, patients get two injections every 6 months.[4]
Evidence behind the approval:
The approval rested on the Phase 3 PURPOSE 1 and PURPOSE 2 trials.
One trial enrolled 5,300 cisgender women and compared Yeztugo with daily Truvada pills. It found zero infections in the Yeztugo group, and the trial was stopped early.[2]
The other trial included a broader population. It showed Yeztugo cut infections by 96% compared with background rates and by 89% compared with Truvada.[2]
Other details:
The list price is $28,218 per year.[2]
People must test negative for HIV-1 before starting Yeztugo and before each injection.[5] The product also carries a boxed warning.
